passage:
Dear Bhavna Didi,
You asked on the phone why I sounded like a news reader. I think it's because I'm performing all the time now.
At home I'm the good son. I say yes to the coaching Papa chose, I wear the shirt Mummy likes to family functions, I pretend I don't want the photography workshop. Then at night I edit photos with the door locked.
Nobody shouts. Papa just goes quiet for days if I disagree, and Mummy says, "After all we've sacrificed." So I've stopped disagreeing. I hide instead.
Last week I read that this has a name: love with a condition attached to every choice. Seeing it written down made me cry in the library.
Would you come with me to talk to Mama? He's the only elder Papa really listens to. I don't want to lose them. I also don't want to lose me.
Yogesh

qa.q: What does Yogesh do at night with the door locked?
qa.a: Yogesh edits photos at night with the door locked.

qa.q: What did Yogesh feel on seeing the pattern written down?
qa.a: He felt relief and grief together; seeing it named made him cry in the library.

qa.q: Which step Yogesh asks for could help, and why?
qa.a: Asking Bhavna Didi to come with him to talk to Mama, the elder Papa listens to, brings in support so he can stop hiding and speak up.

qa.q: What might Bhavna Didi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: She may feel moved and worried, finally understanding why he sounded flat on the phone, and glad he trusted her with the truth.

grounding: A young man loved by his family feels each choice may cost their approval, hides his photography, and names the pattern as a first step.

passage:
Farhan, you know what I did on Sunday? I sat in my best salwar, smiled at a boy's family on a video call, and said I love cooking. I don't love cooking. I love statistics.
My parents are good people. Papa taught me to ride a scooter. Amma cried when I topped the district. But since final year it's "your master's can wait till after marriage" and "don't embarrass us in front of relatives". If I argue, Amma stops eating and Papa says I'm breaking the family's heart.
So I perform. I say yes on calls. I fill the master's form secretly at the cyber café.
Last week Dadi caught me with it. I thought she'd tell. She just said, "Minakshi beti, your grandfather married me at seventeen. I never finished school." Then she said she'd talk to Papa.
I don't know if it'll work. But saying all this to you? It's the first time it feels like mine.

qa.q: What did Minakshi say she loves on the video call?
qa.a: Minakshi said she loves cooking.

qa.q: How does Minakshi feel about performing on the video calls?
qa.a: She feels split and trapped, smiling on calls while loving statistics and fearing that disagreeing would break her family's heart.

qa.q: What turning point came from Dadi finding the form?
qa.a: Dadi, a respected elder, chose to support her and talk to Papa, giving Minakshi an ally inside the family instead of hiding alone.

qa.q: What might Dadi feel on seeing the master's form?
qa.a: Dadi likely feels recognition and an old sorrow, remembering she was married at seventeen and never finished school, and wants a different path for Minakshi.

grounding: A young woman loved by her family performs obedience about marriage while secretly applying for a master's, and a respected elder offers to help.

passage:
Gopika, you asked why I'm always on my phone at dinner at my parents' place. Okay. I'm Pooja, and I think I've become two people.
At home, I'm the daughter who wants to be a bank officer, who doesn't have male friends, who goes to bed at ten. My parents love me so much. My father still peels oranges for me. And every choice feels like it might cost me that.
Outside, I'm doing a design course on Saturdays. I have friends they'd never approve of. I'm on my phone because I'm answering my class group.
I'm so tired of performing. I keep smiling at dinner and feeling sick after.
Last week the college counsellor said a phrase: "loved, but not free." I wrote it on my hand.
Maybe my Nani could help. She always says I should be who I am. I'm thinking of telling her first.

qa.q: What course does Pooja do on Saturdays?
qa.a: A design course.

qa.q: How does Pooja feel at family dinners?
qa.a: Pooja feels loved but exhausted and sick from performing, afraid every choice might cost her parents' approval.

qa.q: What steps might help Pooja?
qa.a: Naming the pattern, as she did with the counsellor, and telling a respected elder like her Nani who might help her talk to her parents.

qa.q: How do Pooja's parents seem to feel about her?
qa.a: Her parents clearly love her, like her father still peeling oranges for her, but they don't see how much she hides.

grounding: A young adult describes being loved by her family yet performing obedience and hiding her real life, and naming the pattern.

passage:
March. Bhupen told his parents he had extra lab classes on Wednesday evenings. Really, he was rehearsing with a theatre group in town. His parents were proud of him, and he loved them. But the one time he mentioned acting, his father had gone silent for three days.
May. At a family dinner, his mother told relatives, "Bhupen will be an engineer like his father." Bhupen smiled and nodded. Under the table, his hand was shaking. He felt like an actor at home too.
July. He couldn't sleep. He called his Tushar Mama, his mother's brother, who everyone in the family respected. "Mama, I think I'm living a lie for them. I'm scared to lose them."
Tushar Mama listened for an hour. Then he said, "You're not a bad son for wanting a say. Let me come on Sunday. We'll talk to your parents together."

qa.q: What did Bhupen tell his parents he had on Wednesday evenings?
qa.a: Extra lab classes.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel at the family dinner in May?
qa.a: Bhupen felt anxious and trapped, his hand shaking while he smiled and nodded to please his family.

qa.q: Who did Bhupen turn to, and why was that wise?
qa.a: He called Tushar Mama, a respected elder, who listened and offered to help talk to his parents on Sunday.

qa.q: How might Bhupen's parents feel if they learned the truth?
qa.a: They might feel hurt at first, but also sad that their son felt he had to hide from them.

grounding: It shows a young adult loved by his family but hiding and performing over months, until he names the pattern to a respected elder.

passage:
Eshaan, you think you're the first one in this family to hide something from your parents? Let your Pema Ani tell you.
When I was twenty, your grandparents loved me like a jewel. Every morning your grandfather put a flower in my hair. And every choice I made, I felt their eyes. What I studied. Who I walked home with. Whether I laughed too loudly.
I wanted to paint. So I told them I was going to extra English classes, and went to an art teacher above the post office instead. For a whole year I performed: the good daughter at home, the painter in secret. I was always tired.
One day my own grandmother found my paint box. She didn't scold. She said, "This is a cage made of love, child. Let's open the door slowly." She spoke to my parents herself.
They were upset for a month. Then your grandfather came to my first exhibition.

qa.q: Where did young Pema go instead of extra English classes?
qa.a: To an art teacher above the post office.

qa.q: How did young Pema feel during the year of hiding?
qa.a: Pema felt loved but constantly watched, and exhausted from performing the good daughter while painting in secret.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Pema?
qa.a: Her grandmother found the paint box, named the "cage made of love," and spoke to Pema's parents herself.

qa.q: How did Pema's parents react at first, and later?
qa.a: They were upset for a month, and later her father came to her first exhibition.

grounding: An aunt recalls being deeply loved yet hiding her painting for a year, and a respected grandmother helping her family understand.

passage: The last bus to Rohtak left in twenty minutes, and Jagdish was still in the practice room behind the music shop, changing out of the band T-shirt he'd worn for his friend Sumit's gig. He folded it into the bottom of his bag, under the ironed shirt his mother liked. At home he'd say he had been at the library. "Why do you do this?" Sumit asked, handing him a comb. "They'd never throw you out." "No," Jagdish said. "They'd just go quiet. Papa would sigh for a week, and Ma would tell Chachi I've changed." He ran for the bus stop in the rain, heart thudding, rehearsing library details. On the bus he texted Sumit: "Maybe I'm living two lives." Sumit replied: "You are. Remember Mehra sir from school? Your dad respects him. Maybe talk to him first?" Jagdish stared at the wet window and, for once, didn't push the idea away.

qa.q: What did Jagdish plan to say at home about where he had been?
qa.a: He'd say he had been at the library.

qa.q: How does Jagdish feel on the bus?
qa.a: Jagdish feels anxious and split in two, heart thudding and rehearsing library details, and admits he may be living two lives.

qa.q: What first step is suggested, and why might it help?
qa.a: Naming the pattern and talking to Mehra sir, whom his father respects, could help Jagdish be honest at home without losing the family's warmth.

qa.q: How does Sumit see Jagdish's hiding?
qa.a: Sumit calls it two lives and believes the family would never throw Jagdish out, so he gently pushes him toward honesty with an elder's help.

grounding: Shows a loved young adult who hides and performs to avoid losing family approval, and is nudged to name the pattern and seek a respected elder.
